external_prereqs: precipitate is an insoluble solid from a reaction

nodes.name: Soap is used up making scum before it lathers
Boiling removes only temporary hardness
Washing soda precipitates Ca/Mg as carbonates
Filtering does not remove dissolved ions; distillation or ion exchange does
Soap is sodium/potassium salt of a fatty acid made from fats and alkali
Detergent is sodium salt of a sulphonic acid or sulphate ester

misconceptions.statement: Hard water is hard because it contains tiny solid stone-like particles.
misconceptions.why: The word 'hard' is read as the hardness of a solid.
misconceptions.fix: Hard water is ordinary clear water with dissolved calcium and magnesium salts. 'Hard' only means soap does not lather easily in it.

probe.question: Hard water looks clear. What makes it hard?
probe.wrong_answer: It has small hard stone particles floating in it.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Hard water is acidic because it contains acid.
misconceptions.why: Students link any 'problem' property of water with acidity, which they know from pH.
misconceptions.fix: Hardness comes from dissolved calcium and magnesium salts, not from acid. Hard water can be neutral or slightly alkaline.

probe.question: What is the pH of hard water likely to be?
probe.wrong_answer: Below 7, since hard water contains acid.

misconceptions.root_belief: unfamiliar water property must be an acid-base property

misconceptions.statement: Hard water is dirty or unsafe to drink.
misconceptions.why: Water that behaves differently from normal water is assumed to be impure or harmful.
misconceptions.fix: Hard water is usually safe to drink. The dissolved Ca and Mg salts only make it difficult to lather with soap and leave deposits in kettles and pipes.

probe.question: Is hard water harmful to drink?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is dirty water full of germs.

misconceptions.statement: Temporary hardness is caused by chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium.
misconceptions.why: Students swap the two lists of salts because both types are just 'Ca and Mg salts'.
misconceptions.fix: Temporary hardness is caused by calcium and magnesium bicarbonates. Chlorides and sulphates cause permanent hardness.

probe.question: Which salts cause temporary hardness?
probe.wrong_answer: Chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar categories can be swapped freely

misconceptions.statement: Boiling removes all kinds of hardness from water.
misconceptions.why: Boiling is the best-known way to purify and soften water, so it is applied to every case.
misconceptions.fix: Boiling decomposes only the bicarbonates, which then settle as insoluble carbonates. Chlorides and sulphates stay dissolved, so permanent hardness remains.

probe.question: Water containing calcium sulphate is boiled for 10 minutes. Is it now soft?

misconceptions.statement: Scum is just dirt and grease from clothes that the soap has pulled out.
misconceptions.why: Students see a greyish curd in the bucket after washing and link it with the dirt they were removing.
misconceptions.fix: Scum is a white insoluble precipitate formed when soap reacts with calcium or magnesium ions in hard water. It forms even in a bucket with no dirt at all.

probe.question: You add soap to hard water in a clean test tube with no dirt, and a white curdy solid appears. What is it?
probe.wrong_answer: It is dirt that was already present in the water, now separated by the soap.

misconceptions.root_belief: Visible residue must be the dirt that was removed
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom observation of soap and hard water practicals

misconceptions.statement: Hard water does not lather with soap because it is oily or thick, and it needs more soap only because it is thick.
misconceptions.why: Students link poor lather with the water's thickness or physical feel and not with a chemical reaction.
misconceptions.fix: Soap first reacts with Ca and Mg ions to form scum. Only after all the ions are used up does extra soap dissolve and form lather. Hard water is not thicker than soft water.

probe.question: Why do you need more soap to get lather in hard water?
probe.wrong_answer: Hard water is thicker, so the soap cannot spread and lather.

misconceptions.root_belief: Physical property of liquid explains chemical behaviour

misconceptions.statement: Detergents clean better in hard water only because they are stronger than soap, not because their calcium salts are soluble.
misconceptions.why: Students see detergent as simply a stronger or more powerful cleaner and ignore the solubility of its Ca/Mg salts.
misconceptions.fix: Detergent Ca and Mg salts of sulphonic acid or sulphate esters are soluble, so no scum forms and the detergent stays free to clean. This is the reason it works in hard water.

probe.question: Why does a detergent lather easily in hard water when soap does not?
probe.wrong_answer: Detergent is a stronger chemical that overpowers the hardness.

misconceptions.root_belief: Stronger chemical simply overpowers the problem

misconceptions.statement: Soap is made from petroleum chemicals like detergent, so both are synthetic and the same kind of substance.
misconceptions.why: Students merge the two products because both are washing agents sold in similar forms like bars and powders.
misconceptions.fix: Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a fatty acid, made from animal fats or vegetable oils heated with alkali such as NaOH. Detergents are usually made from petroleum-based chemicals.

probe.question: What raw materials are used to make soap?
probe.wrong_answer: Petroleum chemicals, like those in detergents.

misconceptions.root_belief: Similar-function products share the same ingredients

misconceptions.statement: In a micelle the water-loving heads point inward toward the grease and the tails point out.
misconceptions.why: Students picture the head as the part that grabs the dirt and so place it at the centre next to the grease.
misconceptions.fix: The hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails point inward into the grease. The charged hydrophilic heads face outward toward the water.

probe.question: In a soap micelle around a grease drop, which part of the soap ion touches the grease?
probe.wrong_answer: The ionic head, since it grabs the dirt.

misconceptions.root_belief: Head part must be the one that grabs
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student misconceptions about soap micelle structure

misconceptions.statement: Washing soda softens hard water by dissolving the calcium and magnesium salts more completely.
misconceptions.why: Students think that a cleaning chemical works by dissolving things, so they assume it dissolves the hardness.
misconceptions.fix: Washing soda (sodium carbonate) reacts with dissolved Ca and Mg ions to form insoluble carbonates that settle as a precipitate. The ions are removed from solution.

probe.question: How does washing soda make hard water soft?
probe.wrong_answer: It dissolves the calcium and magnesium salts fully so they cannot cause hardness.

misconceptions.root_belief: Cleaning chemicals work by dissolving things

misconceptions.statement: Filtering hard water through a cloth or filter paper makes it soft.
misconceptions.why: Students treat hardness as something visible that a filter can catch, as with muddy water.
misconceptions.fix: Hardness is caused by dissolved Ca and Mg ions, which pass through a filter. Only distillation or ion exchange removes them, along with chemical methods such as adding washing soda.

probe.question: Can you soften hard water by passing it through filter paper?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the filter paper catches the calcium and magnesium salts.

misconceptions.root_belief: Filters remove everything unwanted from water
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas of dissolved versus undissolved substances
